title: The preacher of patience
hookLine: an ascetic stays patient while a drunken king has his limbs cut (Jataka 313)

cards: A king falls asleep in his pleasure garden, drunk, with his head in the lap of one of his women. The women of his court, bored with waiting, wander off through the trees and find an ascetic sitting quietly by himself.
They sit around him and ask him to teach. When the king wakes and finds them gone, he goes looking, furious. A word of warning: this tale has violence in it, told plainly.

teach.b: The king demands to know what this ascetic teaches. Patience, he answers; in Pali, khanti. That's why the tale calls him Khantivadi, the preacher of patience.
Second, the test. The king calls for his executioner.

He has the ascetic flogged, and then, one cruelty after another, has his hands and feet cut off, then his ears and nose. After each, the king asks: what do you teach now? Each time the answer is the same.
Third, where patience lives. The ascetic tells the king his patience isn't in his hands or feet, or any part of him a blade can reach. It lies deep within, in the heart.
The king kicks him and walks away, and in the tale, as he leaves the garden, the earth opens and swallows him. Fourth, the last word.
The king's commander comes back to the dying man and begs: if you must be angry, be angry with the king, not with the kingdom.
The ascetic answers that he wishes the king long life, and that people like him do not get angry. Then he dies. The tale is very hard to hear, and it isn't advice to stay where you're being harmed.
It's a picture of a quality pushed to its far edge: patience that doesn't live anywhere the world can cut. What tests an ordinary day is far smaller: a slow line, a loud neighbor, a careless remark.

how: Patience, khanti, is one of the ten perfections in the Theravada tradition, and this tale is told as the Bodhisatta's practice of that perfection.

games.q: the preacher of patience: tap the pairs.
p: drunk and furious in his garden
sat down to hear the ascetic

s: the ascetic says his patience is in his hands and feet
he says it's in no part a blade can reach. it lies deep within, in the heart.
at the end, the ascetic wishes the king long life
people like him, he says, do not get angry.
the king's women went off to hear the ascetic while the king slept
that's what set off the king's fury.

games.q: you're the ascetic, and the furious king demands to know what you teach. what do you say?
games.why: he answers patience, and keeps to that answer through every cruelty the king orders.

practice: Sit, and wait for one small irritation to arrive: a sound outside, an itch, a thought that you're wasting time. When it comes, don't fix it; feel where it pinches, and breathe toward that spot.
See whether the patience lives in the itch, or somewhere further in.

wordCard.voice: Khanti. Patience: what an ascetic named for it keeps while a drunken king cuts him down, and wishes the king long life. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: khanti, patience or forbearance; the ascetic is called Khantivadi, the one who speaks of patience.

carryVoice: Your line: patience holds. Not in the hands or the feet: in the heart. Day eight hundred thirty-two, done.
